query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The addition of low-activation elements such as W, V, or Ti to refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) will result in a low-activation structural material suitable for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors.
generation.intervention: Addition of low-activation elements (W, V, or Ti) to refractory HEAs
generation.conditions: High-temperature (up to 1000°C) and irradiated environment of fusion reactors
generation.mechanism: Optimization of alloy composition to reduce activation and enhance high-temperature mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% reduction in activation level (measured in terms of induced radioactivity) and a 20% increase in high-temperature yield strength (measured in MPa) compared to traditional materials
generation.baseline: Traditional materials used in PFCs (e.g., stainless steel or tungsten)
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 500-1000°C, irradiation dose: up to 10 dpa
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of low-activation element additions on the microstructure and properties of refractory HEAs is uncertain and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabrication and testing of refractory HEAs with varying additions of low-activation elements (W, V, or Ti) in a high-temperature and irradiated environment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the activation level is not reduced by at least 20% or the high-temperature yield strength is not increased by at least 15% compared to traditional materials, the hypothesis is falsified.
